title: Aiuto ottimizzazione disegno cucina | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "via-sarpi", "author_name": "Via Sarpi", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/via-sarpi", "date": "2024-03-01", "text": "Avrei bisogno della vostra saggezza ed esperienza per capire come ottimizzare il disegno di questa cucina. La cucina \u00e8 lineare, molto semplice. I vincoli che avrei: voglio frigo  free standing e non incassato, e non vorrei rompere per spostare i tubi  dell'acqua. Per cui il rubinetto resterebbe dov'\u00e8. E purtroppo \u00e8 al  centro. Inoltre mi piacerebbe massimizzare il piano di lavoro \"in  continuit\u00e0\", senza avere pi\u00f9 spazio \"del necessario\" tra lavello e piano  cottura, o tra piano cottura e muro. Ho previsto un lavello da 70cm, vasca singola integrata nel piano in  acciaio.Il piano cottura (che \u00e8 ad induzione) a me non serve enorme, ma vorrei  qualcosa dove ci stiano comodamente 3 pentole/padelle senza sbattere,  per cui mi \u00e8 stato proposto piano induzione da 80cm.Inoltre, poich\u00e8 non mi piace dover aprire due cassetti per prendere un  cucchiaino, pensavo ai classici tiretti, anzich\u00e8 i cassettoni che ora  vanno di moda. Durante la visita ai vari cucinieri, alcuni mi hanno detto che  lavastoviglie sotto piano induzione \u00e8 un NO fermo, per cui bisogna  spostare, altrimenti si rischia di compromettere funzionamento del piano  cottura. Altri dicono che basta mettere una piastra tra piano e  lavastoviglie e non si verifica nessun problema. Se volessi NON avere la  lavastoviglie sotto il piano cottura, dovrei (rispetto al progetto)  spostare la lavastoviglie a sinistra del lavello (mentre nel progetto \u00e8  a destra). Il dubbio che ho ora \u00e8 principalmente questo: il progetto prevede 20cm  di distanza tra piano cottura e muro a destra. Sono pochini, giusto per  un poggia mestolo. Un'alternativa proposta \u00e8 un'intera base da 60cm, ma  in quel caso sarebbe lontano dal piano lavoro \"in continuit\u00e0\" e sarebbe  un buco nero dove si poggia di tutto. Io in effetti ho sempre sul piano  il bollitore e lo spremiagrumi oppure il frullatore/blender, che  immagino nel progetto andrebbero a sinistra in fondo accanto al frigo. Le soluzioni mi sembra siano poche: rinunciare a parte del piano di  lavoro contiguo, oppure rinunciare alla simmetria di lavello/piano sulle  rispettive basi. Oppure (estrema ratio) rompere e spostare lavello).Il cuciniere che avrei scelto mi ha detto che hanno moduli con passo di  15cm (15,30, 45,60,75,90,105,120). Vi allego il progetto:https://i.postimg.cc/Qx7WzLWS/Schermata-2024-02-25-alle-16-15-37.pngA vederlo ora: 45cm tra lavello e piano mi sembrano troppi, e il piano \u00e8  di 117cm Quindi questa sotto potrebbe essere un miglioramento, con forno e lavastoviglie a sinistra:https://i.postimg.cc/rwJNwdNK/Schermata-2024-02-25-alle-16-16-11.pngqui alcune distanze sono ottimizzate. Considerate che la porta di ingresso in cucina \u00e8 lato  frigo, e il progetto originario prevedeva di tenere il blocco  cottura/caldo/rumore lontano dalla porta (dove c'\u00e8 l'ingresso della  casa). Inoltre c'\u00e8 anche la possibilit\u00e0 che frigo e forno abbiano  acciaio/aspetto diverso, per cui magari uno accanto all'altro non stanno  una bellezza. e questa \u00e8 quella con un po' pi\u00f9 di spazio a destra del piano cottura,  ma troppo poco tra lavello e piano cottura:https://i.postimg.cc/x81SBN5M/Schermata-2024-02-25-alle-16-16-31.png Un'ulteriore soluzione sarebbe quella di avere lavastoviglie a sinistra del lavello ma forno a destra. In questo caso, non porei avere un blocco cassetti da 120cm ma due da 60cm. Lascio la parola a voi esperti! \u00e8 vero che ognuno ha le proprie  abitudini, e uno si abitua anche ad avere 20cm di spazio, ma vorrei  capire se vi viene in mente qualcosa per ottimizzare. Inoltre vi chiedo: per conservare le varie pentole e cose voluminose, avere due blocchi cassetti da 60cm \u00e8 un problema? come li disegnereste (primo tiretto posate e gli altri pi\u00f9 grandi?)? Ogni suggerimento \u00e8 ben accetto grazie in anticipo", "images": []}

title: Growing old roses in cold winter climates | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rosefollyz5", "author_name": "Rosefolly z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rosefollyz5", "date": "2024-03-03", "text": "Years ago when I first found this forum (the early 1990's) there were old rose growers from all over North America and from other countries as well. We were all excited to exchange experiences with our little-known old roses. That eagerness to exhange persists, but in recent years the pool of contributers seems to have narrowed.  What I read seems to be dominated by warm-winter rose growers. Foir a long time I did not notice this shift, perhaps because I myself grow my roses in California, and yes, have a lot of Teas here.  But I would very much like to hear more from growers of old roses who live in zones 5 and 6, even perhaps zone 4.  Once upon a time we had a member who grew a phenominal garden in zone 4.  I was always impressed by his efforts and his remarkable results. I'd like to hear more from growers of old roses who live in zones 5 and 6.  What does well for you?  What is healthy?  What does not, perhaps, require extraordinary efforts to bring through the winter? Please share your experiences.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "le-not", "author_name": "Ross 5b IA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/le-not", "date": "2024-03-04", "text": "It's been only four years that I've been growing roses -- mostly old garden roses -- in Iowa, but I am beginning to be able to make some generalizations about hardiness. ('Madame Isaac Pereire' is singularly lovely, but needs an awful lot of coddling to produce one flush a year.  'Z\u00e9phirine Drouhin' dies back so much that it could not be called a climber, here.)  Most Austins will suffer a lot of dieback, and perform no better than most repeating old roses. I will continue to share my experiences as the garden matures.", "images": []}}

Standards have that thick, bare trunk absorbing all that heat from the sun, pushing sap upward in a steady stream, a much greater amount than most rose canes arising from the base of the bush can push. I found the only thing which stopped the \"bleeding\" from those stock piece cuts was melted candle wax. Elmer's Glue is water soluble. Sap is primarily water. But, melt candle wax over the cut end and it seals it. You have to coat it all over so every possible spot for sap to escape is thoroughly covered. For those real heavy \"bleeders\", you'll find if you make those cuts either early enough in the day or late enough so the sun isn't shining directly on the plant, the sap won't bleed as heavily and you can seal the cuts with candle drippings more easily. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "roseseek", "author_name": "roseseek", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roseseek", "date": "2024-03-09", "text": "@Elestrial 7a you're welcome! Hume isn't difficult to root compared to many others but it isn't AS easy as the multiflora types. That thick cambium really does the job for rooting and budding. It's the tissue which calluses then differentiates and forms roots. It's what heals together with the cambium tissue on the back side of the scion to form new capillaries so nutrients can flow between that of the stock and the scion or graft. If you cleft graft fruit trees, you line up the cambium of the graft variety with the cambium of the stock. Cambium is not only the circulatory system of the rose but it's also stem cell material. If the plant is wounded, it forms scar tissue to seal and heal the wound. If a piece of one plant is inserted into a second plant, it knits together to form new circulatory tissue so the new part becomes part of the whole. If cambium tissue is exposed to cool, dark, damp conditions, it forms callus which then forms roots. When that tissue exists as a thicker layer under the bark in the entire plant, some wondrous things can be accomplished. De la Grifferaie is also multiflora type and it's the stock used to make 8' tall (and sometimes taller) weeping standards. Huey flows sap to about 3', 4' is pushing it. IXL has pushed it over 5'. Burling has created up to 6' tall weepers using Pink Clouds. I budded four buds of  Baby Faurax in a 4' Hume whip in 1994 I rooted and they all took and grew. I gave that plant to a gardening client in 2015 when we sold in Encino and moved to the Central Coast. It isn't a multiflora type, but it's good to at least 4' in length in my experience. How much heat? The San Fernando Valley north of LA gets HOT. It's considered a Zone 9b, as is where I am now, however they are worlds different. The Valley gets warm quickly and remains warm most of the day. Here, we're 9 miles from the Pacific and the ocean breeze keep it rather chilly. Here, I can literally pollinate year round and plant most of the year because the temps remain low enough for germination as well as not so high it cooks the seedlings. Old climate where there was heat.   Here.   I wrap cuttings to get them to callus then plant outdoors to allow them to finish rooting and growing. Huey and Fortuniana would not keep going after being unwrapped. IXL, De la Grifferaie and Pink Clouds do here. I obtained 44 rooted Fortuniana stocks and grafted to them in August when we CAN get heat. Everything simply turned black. The multiflora types all pushed growth. Does that help give you an idea? As for budding, Hume is best for \"T\" buds like Huey, where you have to wait for the stock to really be vigorously growing so the sap is flowing fully and the bark lifts easily. Pink Clouds and the other multiflora types can be \"T' budded, but that thick cambium allows you to chip bud very easily and that is significantly easier for you to learn to do. It requires much less skill and practice. Burling has long promoted Pink Clouds because it remains in condition for budding much of the year. The heat lovers are best when the heat is highest so the sap is flowing fully. There are many tutorials on line how to chip and \"T\" bud. I have a blog post about it here, with photographs. http://pushingtheroseenvelope.blogspot.com/2014/11/chip-budding.html There are a number of other posts on my blog about what I'd budded with photos of how they turned out. And, if you're interested in wrapping cuttings for rooting, you can start here and then scroll forward to glean the discoveries and suggestions as they revealed themselves. title: another reason to keep bread in the freezer | Houzz Forum

The guest bath toilet is farest from the septic tank and the piping for it has to travel the whole length of our house to get to septic. House Hacking Dubious as it might sound, house hacking is a clever way to live in your home and earn from it. The basic premise of this strategy involves buying a home and renting out part of it to a tenant. The rent from your tenants helps you with your mortgage payments and build equity in your home. If your home is paid for, renting out an extra room, basement, or attic is a great way to supplement your income. This strategy works best if you have a big home with at least two rooms. This can be: \u00b7   A multi-family property. \u00b7   A duplex or triplex. \u00b7   An accessory dwelling unit (ADU). The great thing about this strategy is that you can purchase a home with a small down payment. Paying off your home loan is simple due to the rent you receive each month, along with the tax breaks. Once your mortgage is paid off, you can sell your home for a higher value and consider buying a bigger one. Depending on your preference, you can do long-term rentals or use the extra space for short-term rentals via platforms like Airbnb. Ensure you adhere to the zoning laws or rules set by the Homeowners Association (HOA). 2. Fix, Then Flip You\u2019ve probably heard of fixer-upper homes, but now you can profit from them. Home-flipping is a growing property investment strategy that entails buying an underpriced property, renovating it within a budget, and reselling it for a higher price. This idea works best if you have a sizable upfront capital to buy a home (even if at a discounted price) and the means to fix it. Flipping homes is not as simple as you might believe, but it promises excellent returns once the property undergoes a cosmetic upgrade. You\u2019ll also need to stick to a timeline and stay organized so that you don\u2019t hold on to the property long after its makeover. Taking longer to sell a flipped home leads to higher holding costs. Live-in Flip: A subset of the \u201chome-flipping\u201d investment strategy is the \u201clive-in flip\u201d. Unlike a traditional flip, you live in the home you\u2019re remodeling. This is a good way to save money on overhead costs. You\u2019ll also enjoy tax benefits with this method since the home is your primary residence. Once you flip and sell it, you\u2019re exempt from paying capital gains tax under the Section 121 exclusion. You only qualify for this exclusion if you have lived in the home for over two years. If you choose a live-in flip, you may qualify for an owner-occupied mortgage. This type of financing offers lower interest rates and requires smaller down payments. 3. Buying Rental Properties Buying properties and leasing them for residential and commercial purposes remains one of the most popular investment strategies even in 2024. The national median rent for a one-bedroom home is $1496. Despite the slight downtick in rental rates over the past year, they are expected to recover by 2025. The national sentiment toward homebuying appears to be low presently, indicating there will continue to be a demand for rental homes.   Renting homes is a great way to earn extra passive income while benefitting from tax breaks. Of course, homeowners who rent will incur a great deal of repair and upkeep costs throughout the year. But the good news is that you can claim these deductions as the owner of a rental property. Aside from the tax breaks, you enjoy a steady cash flow while your property appreciates over time. If and when you decide to sell it in the future for a \u201clike-kind\u201d home, you can sidestep capital gains taxes via the 1031 exchange. When renting your property, you can consider two types of rentals: Short-term Rentals If you\u2019re averse to fixed, long-term leases, consider short-term rentals for your home. More vacationers are now choosing local homes over hotels for their stays, and your home can be one of them. Long-term Rentals A more traditional approach is a long-term rental with a fixed one- or two-year lease. This ensures a steady cash flow each month, especially if you find a dependable tenant who pays on time. Long-term rentals also avoid the hassle of dealing with different tenants each week, making it a truly passive form of investing. 4. Invest in Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) Managing an actual property can be overwhelming, especially if you\u2019re a new, small-time investor. A real estate investment trust allows you to invest in properties without the hassle of managing them yourself. REITs, as they\u2019re known, are companies that own commercial properties. REITs are similar to mutual funds, which pool money to invest in various equities. REITs pool money to create a varied portfolio of income-generating properties. When you acquire a REIT share, you become an investor and get a dividend. Unlike tangible real estate properties, REITs are liquid investments you can sell for instant cash. They trade on the stock exchange and are publicly listed. REIT companies are beholden to distribute at least 90% of their profits via dividends to their investors each year. As a result, investing in a well-performing REIT can yield definite profits. 5. Real Estate Bonds Real estate bonds are another passive investment technique that offers a chance to earn a fixed income. Think of real estate bonds as a type of \u201cIOU\u201d. You\u2019re the lender here, while the borrowing account is typically a government agency or a corporation looking to invest in real estate projects. In essence, you\u2019re lending funds to the borrower for a predefined period. The \u201cbond\u201d outlines the terms of this loan agreement. Investors who buy real estate bonds receive: \u00b7   A fixed income, aka regular interest payments. \u00b7   Original sum or capital lent upon maturity. Here\u2019s how real estate bonds can benefit you: \u00b7   Principal preservation. \u00b7   Fixed income. \u00b7   Hedge against inflation. \u00b7   Diversification. Maximize Your Real Estate Returns in 2024 with These Strategies If real estate is your investment of choice, the five strategies listed above provide active and passive investing options in 2024. title: How does the company handle a loss like this | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2024-03-08", "text": "I am having carpet installed on my stairs, with matching area rugs on the small landings. I had to wait some time for the carpet because it was special order, and in the intervening time, my cabinet maker had a major job on hold and was able to take on my kitchen, so, briefly, my carpet was held at their warehouse for over a year. They came to do the install yesterday, and the brought in one of the area rugs, and it was not my carpet. I said to the guy that this wasn't my carpet and he went completely white. The area rug was  an Axminster or Wilton weave in 100% wool, from Italy. (not tufted like most carpet these days: the back of a carpet like this looks like a Persian rug instead of having that thick glue coat on it). Having looked at a lot of carpet recently, I am thinking that this was much more expensive carpet than mine, probably $130-150 a yard based on similar carpets they had in the showroom. So the question was, was the wrong carpet sent from the mill, or did this get mixed up with someone else's carpet. It turns out they found my carpet so this was someone else's carpet that they cut into. If you are cutting narrow pieces from broadloom to do steps, making an area rug is not that big a deal. But, if you have a rectangular roll of rug meant to go more or less whole into a rectangular room, or large area rug, then cutting a hunk out of one corner could essentially ruin the entire yardage. And it seems that's what they did. I know there is such a thing as errors and omissions insurance, but isn't that for when a claim is made by a customer? Who eats the cost of this potentially ruined carpet? I am curious, more than anything else, because they found my carpet and other than it being a significant inconvenience and me having to take off another day of work and delay some other things that were supposed to happen, it will all turn out at the end, for me, anyway.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-747092216", "author_name": "A Mat", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-747092216", "date": "2024-03-08", "text": "I used Neem on my outdoor planted lemon tree, it worked. We went for an annual check-up in January and all was fine. Less than a month later he developed a huge tumor on his chest. X-rays and tests were done. No cancer, blood work all normal, but the x-rays revealed that what was thought to be a lipoma on the surface had in fact penetrated the underlying bone. He did not seem to be suffering. He was eating well, albeit more slowly, and acting pretty normally. I spoke about options with my vet, and we both agreed that we would not try to do anything heroic, but would see how he did and make decisions from there. Last week I went out of town for a few days. I came back last night, and he is visibly worse. He has lost weight, is eating very little and is moving slowly. He was always a big jumper and liked to perch on high things, but I watched him gingerly trying to get off our bed this morning and navigate the stairs, and while he can do all these things, it's a noticeable decline. What I have been struggling with-- and my question to all of you-- is how do you know when it's time? I had to put my last cat down just before her 18th birthday after her body had totally shut down over several weeks and she had gone from 12 pounds to 5. I felt then that I had waited too long, and I decided that any future pets would go earlier, and with some dignity. title: Huge shortfall in budget.. what would you do? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "feedingducks", "author_name": "Heather N", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/feedingducks", "date": "2024-03-10", "text": "Hi there.We've have started a whole house renovation that was to have a very simple and small extension (more of a squaring off of an older weirdly shaped extension completed in the 70s/ 2010s.) The squaring off, though small in meterage, unlocked a much better layout.We've had several bad surprises during our renovation and had to demolish more of the house than we wanted to (nearly all of the extension from the 70s). We've completed the groundworks, foundations, and strip out. What was a tiny extension is now a large double storey extension...We are trying to get more accurate costs for everything that's still to happen, but the shortfall is looking pretty huge. It's a really cool mid-century house, so we wanted to do it justice with nice materials and a good look. Not doing anything mad budget wise, but things like getting custom fronts for Howdens carcasses, getting proper wood floors, good windows, etc. We need to completely overhaul things like insulation, heating system, windows, damp proofing, etc, and the house is now completely stripped out so has no kitchen bathrooms floors ceilings heating etc.There are 3 levers we could pull1. Try to trim the costs on every line item. So not go for Ufh/ ASHP, not have wooden floors, have uPVC windows, the cheapest kitchen and bathroom, etc etc. This feels uncomfortable because we know we'd still be spending a fortune on things we wanted to replace from day one, and if we ever had to sell, we might be negatively impacting value2. Try to keep the quality, but not rebuild the area that has been demolished. This is uncomfortable because we lose a study (I WFH), a dining room that was connected to the kitchen, and a first floor terrace, and the house is quite a bit smaller than when we started3. There's an area on the ground floor we were planning to turn into an annex to Airbnb, to help chip away at the mortgage. We could just do the essentials (floor, UFH, brick up garage door, replace windows) but leave electrics kitchen bathroom and all the finishing work until later. This is uncomfortable because the Airbnb income was part of our repayment plan, although we'd hope to still make things add up without it. We don't actually need this space, so it could just sit empty, as long as it doesn't ruin the thermal performance of the house. It could be used as a study if we do windows flooring and have temporary lighting. It's on the ground floor, and the kitchen is on the first, so wouldn't really work as a dining room.While we are waiting for numbers, we aren't sure how big the shortfall is, but it's likely to be pretty huge. I know we have no moral entitlement to getting things done the way we originally wanted them... It's just hard to know which way is best to compromise!Strategically, which lever would you pull to bring costs down significantly?Thanks for any advice", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jonathandb1972", "author_name": "Jonathan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jonathandb1972", "date": "2024-03-10", "text": "You need to see a breakdown to work out where the costs will go.   But given you have started you have to press on so the house is mortgageable and saleable should your circumstances change and you want to sell. In my opinion having a gas boiler and radiators and a \u00a315,000 saving over an ASHP and UFH is a no brainer. I think you also need to be realistic about the rental income.   It may be that you have a USP such as being in the middle of a cycling or walking area and therefore possible to get good occupancy.   But if the reality is that your Air BnB would be a garage conversion overlooking your drive, in the middle of a residential area then your competition is budget hotels who will charge very little for a room bigger than a garage and give a cooked breakfast in the morning.    So if you are projecting low rent and 35% occupancy (or less) then it could take more than 4 years to pay for the garage conversion leading to the conclusion that you should leave it as a garage.  Or you might even conclude that a replan is in order and the kitchen can go downstairs reducing the need for an upstairs extension and roof terrace. And then you should be looking at the finish and deciding where to allocate funds.   For instance windows- since UPVC is a part of most streetscapes I don\u2019t think there  is a problem considering them- especially if this is what is in many of the neighbours houses.    Bathrooms- your plan probably has new bathrooms but could you continue to use the existing bathroom for the next few years and add a suite to your new Ensuite later? And you can get a quality kitchen with lots of appliances at a lower price point by buying second hand.   There are lots of sites that specialise in this. The tip would be to buy a kitchen that has far more units and appliances than you need.", "images": []}}

title: Seasonal stress crack above a door - tips to handle or hide? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "neonzeus", "author_name": "neonzeus", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/neonzeus", "date": "2024-03-10", "text": "I moved into this 35 year old, nearly 3k sq ft. home in NE Ohio about 6 years ago when I retired.  It's been fully renovated top to bottom.  One of the guest rooms on the 2nd floor has a long, thin stress crack at a top of the door frame to the crown molding.  A structural engineer has checked the home, by the way -- and found no structural issues.  Since I've owned the home, I had the crack (1) spackled/painted (it recurred in March); repaired again with a special flexible product recommended by the handyman & painted (it recurred in March); and (3) last year I had the drywall replaced & painted (the crack has just shown up again in the new drywall).  The door to that particular guest room also sticks a tiny bit in the Spring, even after being shaved down.  No other stress cracks or door issues in any other room.  Any permanent suggestions -- besides just closing the door to that room and having a glass of wine LOL?  Any ways to deal with it, short of wallpapering the wall or entire room?  Thanks for any suggestions.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "ci-lantro", "author_name": "ci_lantro", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ci-lantro", "date": "2024-03-10", "text": "I would have another go at repair.  Repair in March when the house has dried out from seasonal heating. I have taken two similar approaches to repairing seasonal cracks over doorways and both have been successful. Seal the cracked edges of the drywall with Gardz.  Fill the crack with Sashco's Big Stretch caulk.  Cut a piece of medium weight non woven interfacing, the sew in type, not the iron on,  to cover the crack with 2-3\" margins.  Use Super 77 to adhere the interfacing to the wall.  Prime the patch with pigmented shellac.  Then use drywall mud to feather the patch into the surrounding drywall.  Prime with Gardz or a good quality drywall primer.  Paint. This^^ patch has held up for several seasons. (I had all of these products on hand.) Last spring, I used Abatron Krack Kote (kit) on two more above the door cracks.  So far, those have held up also. Lowe's stocks Big Stretch caulk.  PPG's Top Gun 400 is a similar product (available at Pittsburgh Paint stores) and is both more user friendly & a bit less expensive than Big Stretch (when I last purchased it.)    Gardz is a Zinsser product, widely available.  Super 77 (contact cement in spray form) is a 3M product. Can you zoom out so we can see that in context. That looks to me like sanded cedar beveled siding. You can replace sections (usually you want to replace entire boards). The boards aren't cheap - but it's a good intermediate repair. A marginally skilled carpenter can do it. Then you will prime the bare wood and probably paint the entire exterior. The importance of this fact is the first part of this question. Second part is deciding on a window configuration to mask the faucet off-set if we keep the current cabinet layout. We are in the position of not centering the sink due to 1) Having previously ordered non-returnable cabinets to fit an entirely different layout, and 2) This layout maximizes the usable and functional volume for the kitchen base cabinets, as well as maximizing the usage of the cabinets we already ordered. Now, if we were to change the cabinet configuration solely to center the sink with the window, I would need to discard the 36 inch 2-drawer base cabinet to the left of the sink, and order a 30\u201d base instead. But, that would mean not only storage loss, but would require two additional 3\u201d dishwasher end panels on both sides to the right of the sink to compensate for the 6\u201d of visible dead space on that wall caused by the smaller, 30\u201d drawer base to the left of the sink.  This solution is not ideal for me at all, BUT, depending on how big a deal it is to have the faucet sticking up in front of the window 6\u201d off-center\u2026. perhaps I would consider it.  Please give opinions on that! My kitchen designer feels that having the faucet off-center is compensated by the fact that we made everything else very symmetrical.  The window is centered on the wall.  The wall cabinets to either side of the window are the same size, creating symmetry. Lastly, the island is centered with all that.  The view out the window will draw the eye as it is a nice view. This kitchen opens to the dining area and living room, so when one looks across at the kitchen and out the window, you will see the symmetry of the above mentioned things, with only the faucet sticking up and being up to 6\u201d off-center. Perhaps not terribly important??? The second part of this is getting the right window configuration. It\u2019s been suggested that I avoid a window that has window panes or lines that make it obvious that the faucet doesn\u2019t hit center. Need to get something that masks that as much as possible. This window space is 76\u201d length X 36\u201d High. I will leave about 10\u201d between the countertop and the bottom of the window frame, and put backsplash there behind the faucet. Doing one big picture window, single pane is one option; but, I\u2019m not a fan of the solid piece-of-glass look, plus the fact you can\u2019t open the window at all. Still an option, though, if aesthetically it\u2019d be better\u2026. The designer is suggesting a single pane across the bottom expanse to camouflage the off-center faucet, but then make it shallow at maybe 18\u201d deep (half the depth of the 36\u201d window space), and the put 3 casement-type windows across the top that can be opened via hand cranks. Open to any other window configuration suggestions as well and all thoughts regarding the importance of the faucet being centered. title: How to avoid nightmares after tv | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "feathers11", "author_name": "Feathers11", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/feathers11", "date": "2024-03-12", "text": "I have long avoided horror movies. They are too terrifying for me, and I have a hard time shaking their images from my mind. Any sort of intense movie bothers me. I remember watching Pink Floyd's The Wall with my older brother when I was in middle school, and I had nightmares for weeks. Any war movies make me anxious--I had to watch/assess The Deer Hunter for a class in graduate school, and it was one of the most difficult assignments because it required repeated viewing of the most disturbing scenes. I've never mastered the art of turning off my empathy after a movie is finished. This happens with non-horror tv, too (I binged Hometown a few months ago, and Erin and Ben Napier made guest appearances in my dreams). I had an easy weekend, and I wanted to watch something entertaining. I landed on All the Light We Cannot See. What a lovely series, and I finished it last night. But then I dreamt about the Nazi protagonist with the creepy eyes, and I felt unsettled all morning. I've researched how to avoid nightmares, and the usual focus is not eating before bed, avoiding caffeine/alcohol, etc. I've tried meditation before bed, light reading, etc. Nothing consistently works, except to not watch tv in the evenings. On the one hand, that's a good thing, I guess. But I miss out on a lot of entertainment--I'd only seen one of the movies nominated for an Oscar. Anyone else have strategies to avoid nightmares?", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "a1an", "author_name": "a1an", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/a1an", "date": "2024-03-12", "text": "With my new roses hitting year 6, I've gone full bore with experimentation. Year 1, just deadheaded Year 2 - some light pruning In my mind, the more leaves, the more food Year 3 and 4. I was following Heirloom's video, knocking them down to 10-16 inches and leaving like 6 - 7 canes left.. Fast forward to Year 6 now. Some roses, I have literally removed some portions of the mini stumps and may have like 2 stumps and left only last  3 canes left. We shall see by reducing all the older stuff, will new thick stems like last year shoot up. In others that are not as vigorous, I have just pruned to about 18 inches high and leaving some framework but also removing some more older stems as well. I can:should probably remove more canes but right now I want flowers so the canes shall stay. In other roses, I have left them much higher than previous years, with the finished pruning at the 26-32 inch high mark as the 1st growing height for the season. In other roses, which was mainly putting out weeper canes until Year 5 hit, strangely these now have the best foot forward this season.. No WYE canes. Just a nice circular open framework with like 7-8 good thicker stems in a nice perfect circle as as a framework. The biggest step I suppose is I cut much harder overall. Some is going to be we shall see....as I cut everything just short of leaving the *2 stumps* and 4 newer canes. It looks pretty bare and grusome but I hope it recovers. It others, I wasn't shy and I either saw cut some older stuff, but mainly broke out the loppers and cut away some that I never would have had the courage to do.....All mainly in the name of removing old, hopefully rediverting energy and hopefully shifting focus to new young strong canes. Seeing a few strong stout canes that shot up 3/8 thick and 5 feet+ easily last year is giving me the extra push that hopefully.....something will grow and replace everything I've cut from the soil or emptied out the framework I'm in Year 3 of my standards and I'm still a bit shy about pruning hard on these....although videos appear to prune them dang hard. All the buds are leafing and I can see more clearer than pre leaf. I've looked at the leaf out and I don't think I will prune more for shape or size with the only note to say is that in all the videos I've seen on standards, they all seem to leave like 2 buds from last year and then prune the rest off. - aka, leaving like 3-4\" of  growth from last year. I suppose this year is where I can say I've cut some really hard just to see if removing energy will allow it to refocus energy from below out. title: "The year's at the spring, And day's at the morn..." | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2024-03-12", "text": "Well, officially it's not quite spring yet, but in fact, the season is here.  We got a foot of rain over a period of two or two and a half weeks, more than I've seen in years; and it fell strongly and constantly, allowing the water to soak in.  Now the sun has come out, illuminating a soft, washed, brilliantly green landscape.  The drainages are full; the Chiavenna in the bottom of the valley is roaring.  The plants have gotten all the water they need, and I'm expecting wonderful results. Of the roses, all the warm climate kinds are full of new growth and buds.  'Mme. Antoine Mari' and 'Mrs. B.R. Cant' have been trying, largely unsuccessfully, to bloom for a while now, starting during the unseasonably warm and dry February that preceded the start of the rain.  'Sanguinea', always the first to open anyway, has been flowering since the same time, not allowing herself to get squashed by all the water coming down.  She is a most beautiful sight, now about twenty years old, spilling down the escarpment and, unfortunately, winning her battle against the equally beautiful and amazing ceanothus.  The sweet violets are in flower all over, the snowflakes in the woods opening, more early narcissus have formed buds, the dog-tooth violets all survived the drought and are blooming now, the lesser celandines are carpeting swathes of the woods and opening their brilliant lacquered yellow blooms, the squills are sparks of little blue flowers here and there:  increasing:  good.", "images": []}

Ends,  \" all's right with the world.\"   Wouldn't it be nice if all were right with the world?   But I can understand the feeling that it is,  outside in my garden ,  or outside anywhere almost,  or eating a great meal,  or  with my family,   or when a stranger looks me in the eyes and smiles.   All  can seem to be right with the world and we can let that sink in and hang on to it when  the center does not hold. John Muir said something about taking time to look in the faces of flowers. Hooray for rain!", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-339647040", "author_name": "Jilly", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-339647040", "date": "2024-03-12", "text": "(((Lyban))) I\u2019m so sorry for your loss. My heart hurts for you. I also lost my DH after a long and brutal cancer (his second one) and BMT. Since he\u2019d survived the first cancer, I was optimistic he\u2019d survive it again. His death was a shock I was not prepared for. I felt like someone pushed me out of a plane with no parachute. I know the searing pain you\u2019re feeling and wish with all my heart I could make it better. We all have different grief journeys, but what helped me in those early days was finding an online support group to connect with others who were also newly widowed. I needed to connect with those who were in the same timeframe as me, who understood the chaos of my mind as I tried to cope. We went through awful timelines and \u201dfirsts\u201d together. We kept each other as sane as possible. We did a lot of crying together, but also sometimes succeeded in making each other laugh through our tears, even if just for a second. I could get online at 2:30 am and find someone else not able to sleep. It was comforting. In those early soul crushing weeks and months, I was not able to accept that he was gone. I circled through stages of gut-wrenching pain, anger, numbness, intense fear and panic (had my first ever and very terrifying panic attacks), pleading to the universe to bring him back, not being able to eat or sleep, sometimes being taken to my knees with the overwhelming pain. I had to try to survive it second by second. Reminding myself to breathe. Then I progressed to minute by minute, then hour by hour, then days, and then months. Later on, it helped me to connect with widowed people who were years ahead of me. It gave me hope that I could somehow survive what felt like my world ending. Try not to look too far ahead, it\u2019ll only be overwhelming \u2014 try to get through each moment being as kind and gentle with yourself as you can. title: Water Filtration | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lindsey-brady11", "author_name": "Lindsey Brady", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lindsey-brady11", "date": "2024-03-13", "text": "We are in the middle of a whole home remodel and need to make a decision on water filtration.  We are on a private well.   We had the water tested twice (1st time sent to a lab, 2nd time local plumber).  The house is 3,800 sq ft with 4 bathrooms & will have 6 people living there.   All 4 bathrooms were remodeled so our goals are to 1) protect the new and original plumbing & fixtures, 2) safe drinking water. pH:  6.5  (lab) / 6.0 (plumber) Hardness:  16.1 mg/L (lab)  / ~ 2.0 grains (plumber) Well Flow Rate:  a bit more than 11 gallons/min Plumber & water treatment company recommended an acid neutralizer to raise the pH.  They said this will increase the hardness and recommended adding a softener as well.  I've been looking at the Fleck acid neutralizers that backwash.  There are a lot of choices. I would appreciate any specific model recommendations based on our stats and needs.  As well as any additional feedback!    Thank you!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/93721fd505f1c17b_2523-w500-h685-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-03-14", "text": "This is all borderline: Your lab is showing slightly less than 1 grain per gallon hardness - which is the definition of soft water. Your plumber is showing 2 grains - not very different from lab and within the limits of accuracy of his test kit. Neither reading would prompt me to install a softener. I understand that you believe that once the neutralizer has been added, the hardness will go up - thus the softener. The lab is testing the PH at 6.5 - which is the bottom recommended by the EPA (under 6.5 calls for treatment). The plumber is measuring 6 - but again not very different and within the limits of his test kit. I think you could be fine not treating this water. Keep in mind that any treatment that you do adds in more maintenance and such and so using a minimal amount of treatment has a lot of advantages. Here's what I would do: I'd completely plumb this so that I had the option of adding a neutralizer and softener - so with the bypass loops, drains, power etc. - but I'd hold off on installing anything. If you add a neutralizer later, I'd check the hardness after that's in service and see where it is. If you need to change the PH of the water - it's not going to be by much. Ditto with the water softener.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "lindsey-brady11", "author_name": "Lindsey Brady", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lindsey-brady11", "date": "2024-03-14", "text": "@jakethewonderdog Thank you so much for your reply and input.  It's interesting because last night my husband and I were talking about not doing anything - because the house is 50 years old.  There have been a few places when remodeling the bathrooms where there was blue corrosion all over the pipes.  But the remaining copper *seems* to look okay - the plumber cut into one at the sink and he said the insides looked good. Our concern is the possibility of messing up a new tankless (gas) water heater that we are having installed if the water is acidic.  Knowing we are installing a tankless system on well water, would you still leave it for now but plumb it (primarily the discharge pipe is what needs to be plumbed in before we sheetrock I think?) in case we add it later? The units will sit in an unfinished  \"mechanical room\"", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-03-14", "text": "Check with your water heater  install manual for the acceptable water pH limits. For example, the Rheem tankless shows the range of 6.5-8.5 as acceptable. Use the lab results rather than the plumber results. At two grains per gallon or less, I would not be concerned about the tankless water heater. If you had hard water, my answer would be different. Be sue that the tankless heater is installed with a set of service valves so that cleaning it is relatively easy - which is a best practice no matter what the hardness level. Again, I would go ahead and plumb everything so you have that option later - so you just have what is known as a softener loop, but no softener. Generally, the softened water excludes outdoor faucets and possibly the cold water in the kitchen. BTW: With a well, you should test your water every couple of years for contaminates - since nobody else is doing that for you. Things can change: these might be farm chemicals, feedlot runoff, an industrial plume that has migrated, etc. You can get the pH confirmed to be 6.5 or above when you do that.", "images": []}}

Keim, Romabio, Limeworks.us, Beeck are some US sources.  No I dont work for them! title: They got me - scammed. TSA Lost and Found alert | Houzz Forum

Really frustrating because I was very early for my flight and the TSA line was oddly quiet. Anyway, despite having the \"Find My\" app on my phone, which is always bugging me (a few days ago it warned me I didn't have my laptop when it was behind me in the car), I had no idea it was missing until I landed. We are leaving for an international trip tomorrow morning and I really wanted to bring it with me--- I have a report to write while I am gone, and also all our travel info in a file that'd be hard to read on my phone. I googled the airport TSA Lost and found and three or four websites crop up.  I click on them and find out none of them are the airport or TSA, they are private companies. I finally get the phone number for the actual TSA --- not a human --- and it leads me to an online form and says \"allow 3-5 business days for our reply to your request.\"  Whaaaaa? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2024-03-14", "text": "erasmus, both HMF and Palatine's web site say \"2-3 ft\", so I presume HMF got that info from Palatine, which appears to be the major source for this rose. title: A tale about organizing ... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "theresa-peterson82", "author_name": "Theresa Peterson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/theresa-peterson82", "date": "2024-03-15", "text": "When I was younger /newly married, I bought a long plastic box that could slide under my bed -- used it for wrapping paper.  It worked fine ... but in the last 5-6 years I've become dissatisfied with my wrapping storage, and stuff was kinda all over my house:  Empty gift bags in the dining room chairs, rolls of paper behind the bedroom door, a whole bag of unopened Christmas paper and ribbons in the guest room closet and who knew what in the attic.  I wasn't even using the plastic box. Then on Pinterest I saw a really cool cart filled with wrapping paper -- oh, so cute!  It was a three-drawer Elfa cart on wheels.  Ohhh, I wanted it!  But the cart was $200.  Nooo.  So I kept looking, and I found similar organization systems using three-tier carts from Michaels /Hobby Lobby in the $30-40 range.  That's acceptable!  So I started studying the various Pinterest models, trying to decide what'd work best for me. The more I planned this project, the more I realized the cart would be inferior to the box under my bed.  I'd have to store it in the coat closet, which would mean moving some things that already \"live\" in that spot.  The cart would only hold 8-10 rolls of paper, and they'd be on the side of the cart ... maybe a bit unweildy during movement.  And it wouldn't be dust-proof.  And, honestly, I don't wrap that many gifts! Fortunately I figured out --  before I spent any money -- that this project would've been a disaster.  Instead I gathered up allll the wrapping items from around the house.  When I saw it allll piled up in my living room, I realized the problem was over-consumption and failing to use what I had (which happened because stuff was all over the house, and I didn't know what I had). I removed a large stand-up box of Christmas paper from the attic ... the paper was yellowed and wrinkled and full of Disney characters like Pocahantas, so it was clearly about 15 years old.  And the box had spiders in it.  Straight to the trash.  Two shopping bags with 8-10 rolls of unopened paper each + various accessories.  Lots of empty gift bags + tissue paper.  I found a box of gift bags in the attic ... most so old that the glue had failed /they were split open.  How'd I get all this stuff? I kept what'd fit in my plastic box.  I discarded extra-long jumbo rolls that wouldn't fit.  I rolled some paper \"together\" on the same roll to save paper -- all similar papers.  The box is crammed full /holds about 25 rolls of paper. title: Poems of grief and remembrance | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "cawaps-gw", "author_name": "cawaps", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cawaps-gw", "date": "2024-03-15", "text": "Annie Deighnaugh posted a poem on Lyban's thread about her DH that had me thinking of the poems we used at the funeral for my mom and my dad. I didn't want to divert Lyban's thread, but I'd like to share, and hear from others what poems and writings they have found meaningful and healing. For my dad's funeral, we used Crossing the Bar, by Alfred, Lord Tennyson. My dad was in the merchant marine for a while after his stint in the army and before settling down as a farmer. Sunset and evening star, And one clear call for me! And may there be no moaning of the bar, When I put out to sea, But such a tide as moving seems asleep, Too full for sound and foam, When that which drew from out the boundless deep Turns again home. Twilight and evening bell, And after that the dark! And may there be no sadness of farewell, When I embark; For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place The flood may bear me far, I hope to see my Pilot face to face When I have crost the bar. For my mom, we use a poem we found among my mom's clippings from when she was in nurse's training, and was uncredited. Mom worked as an RN most of her adult life, except for 10 years she took off when we were little. The last two stanzas really got me. I Am a Nurse I am a Nurse, that gives me pride\u2014 A pride beyond all measure; And happiness down deep inside That makes my work a pleasure. There may be, in some other field, A greater cash attraction; But none, I\u2019m sure, could ever yield My inner satisfaction. I greet each day the rising sun With never-failing verve, For I will know, when work is done, The joys of those who serve. I know, too, that distress and pain Are suffered for a spell. But realize that soon again By far the most get well. I hear the newborn babe\u2019s first cries\u2014 Real music, of the best. I watch a happy mother\u2019s eyes The while she gives her breast. I note the raging fever\u2019s drop As modern drugs take hold; And see the tears of loved ones stop As good news we unfold. And I\u2019ve been loved by many men; For men love those who tend them; And though that love was fleeting them And fickle, I\u2019ll defend them As well as others who forgot My ministrations to them. I\u2019m grateful that is was my lot To render kindness due them. I\u2019ve spent the black hours of the night Holding a fevered hand. To help those in their tortured fight Makes me feel big and grand. We cannot always save their lives, Despite the care we bring; But I learned, when that time arrives, In Death there is no sting. So when my hourglass sand runs low, I\u2019ll tread that final mile With joyful, eager steps, though slow, To meet Him with a smile.", "images": []}

title: Doing Soil Tests on Soil-Less Container Media | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2024-03-15", "text": "University of Massachusetts has a famous soil testing laboratory, and I have been using them for testing of in-ground soil.   I noticed that they separately have an option to test container media.  When does it make sense to test an organic soil mix like 5-1-1? I have an ongoing problem with Azalea and Rhododendron doing well in containers of bark for about 18 to 24 months, after which they go downhill.   Some would speculate that this is because the bark decomposes and ties up nitrogen.   But why guess about that?   Why not just test the soil and find the exact reason the plants are struggling?   The concept makes sense to me.  Am I wrong? When doing a soil test on soil-less medium (e.g., a bark-based container soil) does it make sense to get an additional test done for nitrate testing?    When using services like University of Massachusetts soil test lab, nitrogen testing is not included in the basic soil analysis.  There is a separate test you can order for \"side-dressing\" of nitrogen, but clearly this test is oriented towards commercial farming, to help the farmer understand how much nitrogen to side dress at different times in the season.   The reason  this is confusing is that their list of services includes an option for nitrate testing in a regular soil test, but that option is missing for a soil-less media test: https://ag.umass.edu/services/soil-plant-nutrient-testing-laboratory/lab-services I will call the lab as well, but they are very hard to reach by phone and I would like to get the tests ordered.   So I would appreciate the perspectives of others.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2024-03-20", "text": "My personal perspective is that nutrient testing of container soils - the equivalent to inground soil testing - is unnecessary. What is it supposed to evaluate? Container soils are not comprised of very nutrient dense materials for a variety of reasons and therefore it is incumbent on the grower to provide nutrients as and when needed in the form of regular fertilization. Plus, whatever nutrients may exist are constantly being leached out with the frequency of watering required for container plantings. Any soil test results would immediately become invalid. There are also very valid reasons why better soil labs do not routinely include nitrogen analysis as part of their tests. N is the most mobile of the essential plant nutrients and levels will vary widely by time of day, time of year, recent rainfall and a number of other factors. This makes any evaluation just a momentary snapshot in time and therefore not a reliable assessment. One can safely assume that N is almost always deficient in both inground soils (most) as well as container soils and supplementation in some form will typically be necessary.", "images": []}}

I've been growing trees in containers since the early 1980s and I've found that media which hold a lot of excess water (perched water) are generally not a good choice for trees because the excess water limits the oxygen roots need to function normally. It's particle size that primarily determines how much water a medium can hold. The finer the particles that make up the medium, the more water it can hold. If a medium is based on a large fraction of fine ingredients like peat, coir, compost, composted forest products, ....., it's almost certain it well hold enough excess water. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell' (more reliable than a 'moisture meter'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) works better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half or in several pieces, depending on how deep your pots are. Sharpen both ends of each tell in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell's tip comes out nearly dry. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Squill and the foliage of Cyclamen hederifolium under the persimmon in front of the house. title: Speaking of crankiness | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hhireno", "author_name": "hhireno", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hhireno", "date": "2024-03-16", "text": "My last two experiences at live shows have made me a crankier old lady than normal. It\u2019s hard to enjoy these events when other people are so clueless, a polite way to say rude. 1) We went to see Mnozil Brass, a humorous, Austrian, brass septet at a nice, university theater. In the row in front of us was a family consisting of two 70-ish grandparents, a 40-ish mom, and a 10-ish kid. Immediately before the house lights dimmed for the show to start, Mom handed he kid a full sized Ipad. The kid then looked at a children\u2019s book on the ipad, with the screen in full brightness. After a few minutes, the grandfather tells the Mom to dim the screen brightness a bit. Luckily, the stage was brightly light and the septet is loud and lively, so I could try to focus on that and not the glare a few feet away from me. What if it had been a quiet play, or lecture, or something that wasn\u2019t loud and well lit? After looking at the ipad for a while, the kid then fidgeted in her chair, rested her head on mom\u2019s shoulder, needed mom\u2019s jacket to be draped over her, pushed off the coat and then fidgeted some more. She never seemed to pay attention to the performers. I always assume kids are doing their best, and need to be exposed to different situations to learn to cope. But how did it not occur to the adults that the glow from Ipad would distract others? How did it not occur to them that the kid was not going to be interested in the program and shouldn\u2019t attend? She started using the ipad the moment the group started, she didn\u2019t watch the group and then lose interest. Maybe that event wasn\u2019t the best teachable moment. I did not speak to them because I didn\u2019t want to disrupt others any more than we were already being disrupted. And because it can be dangerous to speak to people who are that rude. It would have been disruptive to get up to find an usher. The venue happened to send me a survey afterwards, and I asked what should have been done in the situation. I have not heard back in over a month. 2) We attended a comedy show in an arena. The whole time the show was happening, 3 openers and a main act, people were up and down out of their seats. More food, more drinks, bathroom breaks, and whatever else was making them get up. A guy 2 rows ahead, seated in the middle of his row. got up three times. A couple to our left disrupted their row twice. I don\u2019t understand this. I paid to hear the comedy, I wouldn\u2019t want to miss some jokes so I ate before we got there, and used the restroom before the show started. I also had my choice of hundreds of seats and booked the aisle. Why didn\u2019t the the jack-in-the-box people book end seats so they wouldn\u2019t inconvenience others so much? Why can\u2019t adults sit still for 60-90 minutes? My husband said this is what happens at sporting events, too. The most galling is they sit still during breaks and timeouts but then get up during playing time. He tells me years ago, people would wait for a break in the play to get up or return to their seats but now its a free for all. Why do so many people just not care or not realize they may be disrupting other people\u2019s expereinces? It  makes me question if I really want to attend public events any more.", "images": []}

title: Real estate commissions:  This may be the end to them as we know them | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mxk3", "author_name": "porkchop_z5b_MI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mxk3", "date": "2024-03-16", "text": "H**z still wonky with the links, so here's the text from the NPR article about it; I wonder how this will affect how homes are bought and sold, particularly for buyers who want to work through an agent: The National Association of Realtors has reached a nationwide settlement that could change the way real estate agents are compensated. Critics say the current system artificially inflates agents' commissions.  For years, sellers have effectively set the commission paid to buyers' agents as a condition of using a multiple listing service (MLS) \u2014 a regional roundup of homes for sale. The combined commission \u2014 shared by buyers' and sellers' agents \u2014 is typically 5% to 6%, which is higher than in most other countries.  There's also a potential conflict in having the home seller decide how much the buyer's agent is paid, since they have different objectives in negotiating a home sale.   Under the settlement, commissions will be subject to more negotiation, which could lower the cost of buying and selling a home. It could also drive some real estate agents out of business. Home sellers can still offer a commission to the buyer's agent, but that will no longer be a condition of using an MLS.  The National Association of Realtors lost at $1.8 billion jury verdict last year and was facing other lawsuits over the commission structure. The penalty threatened to put the organization into bankruptcy. As part of the settlement, the National Association of Realtors did not admit to any wrongdoing but agreed to pay $418 million over the next four years. The settlement still needs approval from a federal judge. The changes to real estate commissions are set to take effect in July.", "images": []}

title: All terrain vehicles can be very dangerous | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "appletonianum", "author_name": "Jeb zone 5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/appletonianum", "date": "2024-03-17", "text": "Hello everyone - I live in the country.  Twenty five years ago I moved to the family farm after my dear grandmother died and have really enjoyed being here.  For the most part.  In the time that I have lived here my experience with off road vehicles has not been all that great.  Here ATVs are known as \"automatic trespass vehicles\" - snowmobiles fall into the same category because somehow the laws that apply to all other vehicles don't seem to apply to these. I have had very drunken and lost ATV drivers show up in the middle of my fields the week they were planted with corn, people on off road vehicles in my woodlands tearing up the hillsides and messing up the creek beds.  I find their tracks everywhere on my property when the soil is wet.  Calling the police doesn't do any good, the offenders will tear up my place and then speed off to someone else's property. Yesterday as I was driving home from visiting a friend at the hospital I was on my street and some kid on an ATV came blasting out of his driveway making a left hand turn right in front of my car.  He was wearing a helmet, but he did not look at all and was totally unaware and oblivious to the fact that I was coming down the street.  I had to slam on my breaks and by then he had pulled out in front of me and we were staring at each other almost head - on.  I laid on my car horn for about a full minute and did the horizontal hand arm slash gesture meaning DON'T EVER DO THAT AGAIN!!!  I almost ran him over and if I didn't see him coming it could have ended very badly - for both of us.  He pulled around my car and I doubt that he really learned anything from the experience.  I was badly shaken by it. What are your views on all terrain vehicles?  I have known enough people myself that have either gotten hurt very badly on them or have died while driving them.  It just doesn't seem worth the thrill they might provide when you end up in a wheelchair for the rest of your life because of a bad decision.  You don't need a seat belt or a license to operate one - there isn't even an age requirement.   Thanks for listening, just needed to rant and I feel better now.  Please drive safely!", "images": []}

I flush the toilet, tank fills but the drip persists, however, the tank remains FULL, no refilling of the tank... period! I decided to flush the toilet and turn the inlet vavle off to see if the drip stops and it didn't. So, I call a plumber. They check the usual suspects and have a thermal detector and sonic hearing device. They came up empty. So, today, I flush the toilet, turn off inlet valve, and no drip. I've repeated this 3x's with success. Is the issue in the toilet or in the wall? It can't be in the wall because water damage would be obvious by now as the toilet is upstairs in the MSTR BATH and no evidence directly below in the living room. This problem has been going on for at least 2 months solid. Just remember, the tank is not refilling, not once. I NEED HELP!!!!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jdpyn2", "author_name": "John 9a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jdpyn2", "date": "2024-03-17", "text": "I have a couple of possible sources for your toilet water drip but I would have thought your plumber would have been specifically looking for my proposed sources....it's just so common I think he would have been looking for it.  I assume the drip IS from the toilet since it stops when you turn off the toilet source water. The answer might be different, or troubleshot differently, depending on the type of ballcock your toilet has....the system it uses to fill and shut off when the tank is full.  If I had to guess, I would say the valve that shuts off the water when the tank is full has a small leak.  When the tank fills, typically, a float rises with the water level and eventually rises high enough to shut off the fill water.  If that valve leaks a bit, the drip will ultimately raise the water level enough to enter the overflow pipe and enter the toilet bowl.....one drip at a time so you won't notice water entering the toilet bowl at that rate.  The easiest way I know to check for this issue is to leave the cover off the tank on the back of the toilet and either watch for the drip....or look to see if the water level rises to the overflow line after some period.  If the drip is very slow, water might even be evaporating from the tank faster than the drip is filling it. One other possibility is very much related.  There is in many/most ballcocks a small flexible line that ends just inside the overflow pipe.  This line helps to refill the toilet bowl as the tank is refilling.  If the drip is coming from this line, the drip will be bypassing the tank and dripping down into the toilet bowl (via an inner route).  You can pull this flexible line out of the overflow pipe and watch it for drips. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2024-03-18", "text": "What  power rating does your microwave oven claim to have? It is unlikely to have suddenly gained performance. Have you checked the timing?  That is, measured with a watch how long it runs vs. what you set it to. Cup handles heat up indirectly from the cup contents, or from having materials susceptible to heating by microwave energy.  It is very unlikely that the same cup had a materials conversion. I like the Austins too and you picked some good ones that will look great against the neutral palette of your house and yard. Some folks do underground sprinklers, but I'm low tech and prefer the sprinklers you haul around with a hose (also easier to control). Elena says she's had better luck and I agree that Olivia can take some shade. If those are the conditions you have (including at least 1/3 of my planting areas), you work with the spaces as needed. If you have pots, there is the potential for adjusting where they are after you see how the sun works in your yard. I've grown nearly all the roses you list except Oxford Girl, Like No Other, Silas Marner and Eustacia Vye. Of those, the only ones I've had do OK in part sun are The Lark Ascending, Lady of Shalott, Olivia Rose Austin and to some extent The Alnwick Rose. Scepter'd Isle I had in full sun but it's robust enough it might do OK. Olivia is a robust and sturdy self standing rose and she gets a lot of people's votes as a favorite Austin. I find she's among the bigger of the roses you list, even more than some that are listed as \"climbers\". Gertrude Jekyl never cleared 6' for me and bloomed rarely if ever in part sun, so she wants full sun to have a chance. James Galway and St. Swithun climbed OK (maybe 6-8') but didn't bloom much at all in part sun, so they like more heat and sun too. There is no separate rose that is Lady of Shalott climbing, just the note from DA that under some circumstances she can be induced to get tall and lanky. By \"some conditions\" that means places like California or England. In our climate, she is notably short, staying no more than 4' tall. That's an asset and she's a wonderful rose, but don't expect her to climb in our zone at all. Probably the same goes for Claire Austin, and there's no climbing form per se for that one either. She is listed with the wildly disparate heights of 5' to 11 feet. In our zone, probably no more than 5-6', California/England, most Austins will get \"octopus arms\" that can climb to 11'. Crown Princess Margareta did get very long thin canes that I wound several times around an obelisk in my yard, so she was genuinely a climber. What she wasn't (for me) was a bloomer. At all. In the 13 years I had her (grafted from DA roses), I got exactly one bloom cycle in one year (2013 if you care to note). Others have had much better luck for bloom including in my region - just stating my results. Zephirine D and Pretty in Pink Eden are both legitimately classes climbers and they can get to a good size in this zone. ZD has a reputation for not liking heat much and being a once or twice (spring and fall) bloomer in hot climates. YMMV, but you might not give her the most prominent spot. I couldn't overwinter PiPE, but others have and like her in my region. For your grandfather's grave, the rose planting is a lovely thought and there are cemeteries in other regions where heritage roses are grown. A couple of thoughts to consider, if you haven't already checked on this. First, ask the site if they support permanent plantings. The cemeteries where my in-laws are buried is very adamant that only artificial or temporary plantings like pots are allowed. I notice in your photo that only pots are visible and nothing else has a permanent planting. You might double check before you get your hopes set on a rose trellis that can only be done permanently. If they won't allow permanent plantings, you might be able to do a pot, but someone is going to have to maintain it regularly including watering. Most cemeteries make policy decisions based on what is easiest to do as a blanket control for neatness and that's why they may discourage or even rip out permanent plantings. Just check! The cemetery is definitely part sun at best so that's where (if you have permission) you might put something like The Lark Ascending or Lady of Shalott in a pot on each side of the grave. Their colors would complement each other with soft color in the shade. The good news is that in your house situation I don't think even those big trees would shade out your roses all day if they're in that central spot with the fountain. On the north side of a house is always less sunny, but that bed is far enough from the house to not be particularly shaded by the house itself. I've found that even my hottest sun bed on the south side of my house gets some shade in the afternoon from a big oak tree about 10' to the west of that bed, and they frankly enjoy a respite from the 8-10 hours earlier of sun. You could try all of your roses in pots for the first year and see how the light patterns change in your yard for the first year before planting. Koko Loko is the one that stands out as needing the most sun of the ones you mention, at least in my yard. Hope this helps! As always YMMV, just sharing other zone 5 thoughts. Have fun! title: Soil high in calcium but End Blossom Rot | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jkhsdsu", "author_name": "jkhsdsu", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jkhsdsu", "date": "2024-03-20", "text": "Hello! Midwest gardener here (zone 4). I did a My Soil test on my 300 sq ft vegetable garden last year and discovered that the soil was high in calcium/magnesium/phosphorus - low in nitrogen. I added a 12-0-0 fertilizer per the instructions. During the last growing season all of my tomatoes had END BLOSSOM ROT \ud83d\ude2d. I know this can be caused by watering issues but I watered consistently as possible. I ended up spraying with an end blossom rot spray but by the time I discovered the rot it was mostly too late for my crop.Fast forward to this year - the calcium/magnesium levels are even higher!! I'm desperate to avoid another year of End Blossom Rot.Any thoughts or suggestions?? Would adding a small amount of iron sulfate help??Thank you so much for your advice!!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2024-03-25", "text": "Nitrogen is not well tested in a soil test. I typically ignore that number. The reason is that soil nitrates are very soluble, and leach rapidly. They also come out of compost to some extent. So at any one time, a soil test for nitrogen is not very trustworthy. That being said, note that many sources say that BER can be caused by over-nitrogenating the soil, though your nitrogen numbers are indeed very low. What's more, it is said that you should only use nitrate nitrogen as the fertilizer nitrogen source. Ammoniacal nitrogen may increase blossom-end rot as excess ammonium ions reduce calcium uptake.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "zhdoo", "author_name": "waiting_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/zhdoo", "date": "2024-03-21", "text": "I inherited some property that has a small rose garden, about 8 bushes. It has been long neglected. I want to keep them but I'm unsure how to approach a couple of them. They have no new canes at all, just old canes with rough grey bark. I'm afraid if I cut them way back they won't have any viable buds under that grey bark or they won't grow new canes from the base and I'll lose them. I've seen them in bloom, one is a chalk-white David Austin type and the other is a red and white swirl that could be my absolute favorite. I have to deal with those first so I can get to those further back in the thicket. Suggestions, other than pull them out and plant new ones, would be appreciated. gary", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hzdeleted-38632450", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-38632450", "date": "2024-03-21", "text": "Gary, I have yet to meet an established (old and neglected) rose that did not recover from a very hard pruning. The roses you describe sound like modern repeat-blooming types, so I believe you\u2019re safe to cut them back to 1 to 2 feet tall and they will regrow. There are always dormant eyes on the canes and at the base of the plant, ready to start new growth when needed. A hard pruning of an old plant is generally rejuvenative, so this is an opportunity to reclaim these roses and build them up with renewed vigor. If these are actually \u201dantique\u201d types that bloom once in Spring (no repeat) then you can still cut them back, but you will sacrifice this year\u2019s blooms.
