Or is it best to just use the white primer? Having wallpaper removed - the walls are in good shape and the walls are white or maybe it is the sealer. Which primer would you recommend prior to applying the SW Aesthetic white paint?? What is your recommendation for a good exterior wood primer from SW. Thanks.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "ci-lantro", "author_name": "ci_lantro", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ci-lantro", "date": "2024-03-21", "text": "Having wallpaper removed Zinsser's Gardz is what I would use.  Gardz locks down any residual wallpaper paste.  Residual paste can play havoc with topcoats.  Previous owner had painted over wallpaper paste (two story staircase and upper level hallway).  Paint had crazed and was flaking off in spots.  So I would never risk a paint job over wallpaper paste without using Gardz. Gardz is a thin white (like skim milk) out of the can and dries clear.  Not recommended to tint Gardz.  I have used flat white paint that I had sitting around to help cover and then topcoating with the new preferred pricey stuff.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "faron79", "author_name": "Faron79", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/faron79", "date": "2024-03-22", "text": "Yes.....do a couple full coats of Gardz!!! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "nippstress", "author_name": "nippstress - zone 5 Nebraska", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nippstress", "date": "2024-03-22", "text": "Not in my experience, but I'm not aware of the science either way. Basal breaks can be rose specific or nutrient-specific, and they can come from underground just fine for those of us who have to bury the grafts. If a rose dies to the soil line, it can be the only way it survives the winter. The most consistent advice I see to encourage basal breaks is to feed the rose some alfalfa in spring. title: Is my soil too high? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "michael-robinson144", "author_name": "Michael Robinson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/michael-robinson144", "date": "2024-03-22", "text": "I recently got some grading done to address water entering my crawlspace. However, from searching the internet, im concerned the soil is too high. Will the soil graded this high negatively impact the foundation / brick siding?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2e3202b805fde608_8318-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0332034b05fde60a_8320-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4872003905fde60d_8323-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/045203ae05fde60f_8325-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d292296805fde612_8328-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a4222cfd05fde616_8332-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c5f23e4e05fde618_8334-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2024-03-22", "text": "Brick is porous. It absorbs the water sitting in the soil which moves upward on the wall, and can lead to the algae growth like you have (probably not enough air movement/sun from behind some removed bushes). If you have improperly installed flashing/membrane/WRB behind the brick the water can get to the wood, and mortar sitting in water can deteriorate. Pests like moisture laden materials. I often see houses in Georgia with soil right against the brick. Really there should be a waterproof membrane (e.g. Henry Blueskin) up just past the grade height. It looks like you needed to raise soil to get a good slope away from house, but that causes the soil to be higher than before. You can pinpoint a height on the wall that grade doesn't go over, then remove the grade to get the slope away from house. It's also helpful to bury downspouts near the house to get them far away (min 10' away), keep the soil below the sidewalk to prevent wash onto it, and make sure there is a well at the crawlspace vents and the well bottom height accounts for puddling. Also, you may need to add a step up to porch.", "images": []}}

title: Fertilizing hosta | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bkay2000", "author_name": "bkay2000", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bkay2000", "date": "2024-03-23", "text": "My hosta were really set back by the stifling heat and low humidity last summer. I think Squash Casserole is the only one that doesn't appear to be smaller than before. I'd like to get them in good shape early in the season, as El Nino might not finish with us before mid-summer. A while ago (probably years ago), there was a discussion on how often to fertilize potted hosta. It was quoting Solberg and someone else. If I remember correctly, the professionals said 1/2 strength water soluble fertilizer every 2 1/2 weeks. Does that seem accurate to you? bkay", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hosta-maker", "author_name": "hosta_maker", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hosta-maker", "date": "2024-03-23", "text": "I use a combo of natural and commercial fertilzer. commercial for faster immediate growth. water soluable tomatoe fertilizer in spring, should be a blue color when dissolved. then blooming fertilizer in mid june to help with seed production. the danger of all commercial is that you wil get salt build up in your pot mix over time, which will eventually stunt them. commercial nurseries can get away with it as they aim to pump and dump. sell them before this happens. the natural part for keeping them in a pot long term is to use composted manures. we keep chickens so i have the used wood shavings manure mix in a pile decomposing with high nitrogen, but also developing sub nutrients as it ferments, adding a little microryzome fungi spores and worm castings to the mix can only improve it. let it cook like a compost for awhile. then to build growth within the pot add the fertilizer compost to the bottom of the pot. add it in thirds. bottom hi nitrogen fertilizer compost, the middle gets straight mini pine bark nuggets for aeration and substrate for root stretch. then the top is your basic pro mix, which has your peat for water retention. then dig a whole in the middle of the pot and plant. the basic idea is the roots will grow and reach down to the lower part of the pot getting aeration along the way. renew the pot mix every three years. when you water them weekly, or more in hot climates, get a water wand with a medium fine spray, water below the leaves, you can even hold the head right down on the soil where it creates a bubble action at the top of the soil. this helps get  oxygen to the roots as slightly mixing nutrients in the pots. when there is not alot of heat stress, let the pots dry back a few days, this lets oxygen back into the pot as well as allowing air pockets in the bark, your next watering should then flush out the gases accumulated during dry back. this is my method, as i have learned thru trial and error.", "images": []}}

title: How long will a Kitchenaid mixer last in the box? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "fawnridge69", "author_name": "fawnridge (Ricky)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fawnridge69", "date": "2024-03-24", "text": "Brand new, still in the factory-sealed box. We bought a 6-quart mixer to have as a backup for our cookie production. In the 14 years I've been baking cookies, we've had a mixer die in the middle of a bake, so we bought a spare when they were on sale two years ago...just in case. My question is how long will last in the box? Are there lubricants that will dry out and need replacement? Are there rubber parts that will harden and not work. Of course, we'll find out one of these days when the mixer that's in use freezes up or won't start, but I'd rather know in advance. title: Asking Google  Bard (Gemini) to write me a story about roses | Houzz Forum

This was the resultIn the heart of a forgotten greenhouse, nestled amongst dusty glass panes and cobwebbed corners, lived a rose named Isabella. Unlike the vibrant blooms displayed in bustling flower shops, Isabella was a Gallica rose, a survivor from a bygone era. Her petals, a deep velvety red, held whispers of forgotten waltzes and secrets shared under twilight skies.Isabella shared the greenhouse with other Gallicas, each a unique shade of rose or purple. There was Clementine, whose apricot blooms held the warmth of a summer sun, and Edgar, a brooding crimson rose, perpetually shrouded in an air of mystery. Every day, they basked in the filtered sunlight, their fragrant whispers carrying tales of a past life.Legends said this greenhouse had once been a haven for royalty. Every bloom held a story \u2013 a proposal whispered beneath a trellis, a heartbroken tear staining a velvet petal. The roses yearned for those days, for the touch of human hands and the sparkle of admiration in human eyes.One warm afternoon, a young boy named Leo stumbled upon the forgotten greenhouse. He had been playing hide-and-seek with his grandfather, the caretaker of the vast estate, and a misplaced ball had led him astray. The sight that greeted him took his breath away. Roses of every imaginable shade, their fragrance heavy in the air, bloomed in a symphony of color.Isabella, sensing a visitor, unfurled a bit further, her velvet petals catching the sunlight. Leo, mesmerized, approached her cautiously. He had never seen a rose quite like her. Unlike the perfect, sterile roses in his mother's vases, Isabella seemed to tell stories. Tentatively, he reached out a finger, and to his surprise, a single thorn didn't prick him but brushed his skin with a gentle touch.From that day on, Leo became a frequent visitor. He brought Isabella tales of the outside world, of vibrant butterflies and playful kittens. Isabella, in turn, regaled him with stories of bygone eras, of grand balls and whispered secrets. They formed an unlikely friendship, a boy and a rose, connected by a shared love for beauty and the magic of storytelling.News of the hidden rose garden spread. People from the village started making pilgrimages to see the legendary Gallicas. Isabella, once forgotten, became a local treasure. Her stories, passed down from Leo, added a layer of magic to her beauty. The forgotten greenhouse buzzed with life once more, a testament to the enduring power of connection and the timeless beauty of a rose.", "images": []}

Some say to seal.  Some say that you don't have to seal, especially if it's Polished.  That it can actually \"trap\" water in the stone and degrade the stone. I also read that if you have iron in your water, it can interact with something in the marble and cause rust.  But I guess this is not a concern if you have a good/professional water softener system. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "chispa", "author_name": "chispa", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chispa", "date": "2024-03-25", "text": "Rust:  the rust is actually in the Marble and turns orange-brown when the marble is exposed to water.  It has nothing to do with how the water is conditioned.  Cheap marble ( China) is more prone to rusting than higher quality marble. You need to seal marble before you grout and then again after the grout has dried.  Sealing it before grouting, or using grout release, helps to clean up the tiles after grouting. Most of the issues with shower floors are due to improper waterproofing and/or sloping of the shower pan. For best results, go to your local independent tile stores for better quality tile and hire the best GC and tile installers you can find.", "images": []}}

title: Drainage solution | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "simplesierra", "author_name": "simplesierra", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/simplesierra", "date": "2024-03-26", "text": "Hi, During constant rain I get pooling at the front of my house. I\u2019m looking for a cost effective solution to eliminate the pooling. https://imgur.com/a/aDOMVfB For this setup, would you suggest a French drain, trench drain or regrade the soil so the water can drain into the existing trench drain? I\u2019ve been recommended two solutions: 1. Cut out section of pathway and install a trench drain leading to the downpipe closest to the fence. Install stormwater pit near retaining wall and connect to downpipe. 2. Install a French drain between the driveway and the concrete path that connects up to the existing trench drain. Also with option two, how would you connect up the French drain with the trench drain? Would you have to cut a hole in the side of the trench drain to connect into? The trench drain drains to a soakwell in the backyard.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2024-03-27", "text": "Because water is draining towards the house porch and pooling, it looks like you need a surface drain on both sides of the sidewalk. I would not cut the porch to install a trench drain, as you will still have water pouring over the front edge of porch to get to this new trench drain (and the porch looks sloped away so all the water will not reach the drain anyway). Also, cutting exposed aggregate finish will not be a clean look. So, you can eliminate cutting the porch as an option. Realize a french drain needs to be deeper within ground to function to it's potential (which might be lower than the existing driveway trench drain outlet so you couldn't connect if so). And has to wait for the ground to be saturated above the french drain \"system\" prior to functioning wholely. But water can still run on the surface without the ground being saturated, like in a rain deluge. So a french drain is secondary to grading properly, but when you can't regrade and have pooling like you do, you have to introduce surface drains. - You can install a trench drain right next to the porch all the way across (piped under the sidewalk to connect each side). Whether this connects to the existing driveway trench drain or bypasses depends on where the drywell is/outlet depth or a daylight opportunity (wasn't clearly understood on existing for that). - Or instead of a split trench drain you can install two catch basins a tiny bit further out from the edge of porch, and regrade the soil so it is all sloping towards the catch basin grates. Note the outlet depth of catch basins would be lower than a trench drain if that matters in how you discharge them. - If you have the depth to gravity drain a french drain pipe (to the drywell or daylight) then I would also install that all the way across. With the house being lower the water coming towards it will have some effect on something over time, whether a crawl space, basement, settling, sogginess of yard, etc.", "images": []}}

title: Fine Cracking in Plaster | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-655173599", "author_name": "ade 12000", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-655173599", "date": "2024-03-26", "text": "Hi, I am redecorating a 1960's home, in one bedroom I have removed the old lining wallpaper from the walls to discover the plaster has various levels of cracking. The majority of the cracks are very fine across entirety of the the walls. Shown in the first 2 pictures. Then one wall has bigger cracks. I would like to paint the walls without using lining paper. Can anybody help me with how to prepare the walls to allow for painting that wont then show up the cracks? I know with larger cracks they will need to be filled but on the very fine ones will a few mist coats prevent the cracks from coming through the end finish? thanks", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6b32699c0602b2d3_2909-w500-h664-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/783266970602b2d5_2914-w500-h664-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ed02459d0602b2d7_2920-w500-h664-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-462192744", "author_name": "Isla Cherry", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-462192744", "date": "2024-04-08", "text": "I think I would ask a painter to comment on the cracks. Hairline cracks are almost impossible to fill before painting and will show through the finished freshly painted wall. It could be settlement, it could be a skim coat cracking, it could be many things. Lining paper sounds like a viable option to me although you said you'd rather avoid it. You could do a test patch. Pick a patch about 300mm sq with a lot of cracks. Paint one coat of your choice (sample pot) over it. Do a second and possibly a third coat allowing drying time of at least a day in between. Observe it for a least a month. This could prove tedious. You could just risk it and paint but the cracks may reappear in your hard work.", "images": []}}

title: updated zone finder | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2024-03-27", "text": "The USDA Plant Hardiness zone is a handy reference to the average severity of winter temperatures at a given site. It, of course, has NOTHING to do with summer gardening. Just FYI, last year the USDA updated these zones, taking climate change into account. They are available, by zip code, at https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/. Interestingly, that site not only tells you what the current 2023 zone is, but also the zone that predated it. We've talked about that here. Not sure if this has already been reported here, but be aware that the GardenWeb zone finder, at https://www.gardenweb.com/zones still gives you the old values, and doesn't seem to distinguish a and b subzones. While it includes a link to the USDA site, the numbers it gives are the old ones. This is not a major error, but is something that people might want to be aware of. I should add that you should be careful about how to use these zones. They're more appropriate to annuals than perennials because these are just AVERAGE winter severities. You can, in time, get winter weather that is VASTLY colder than your listed zone. We've had a good example down here in the last two years. We are at zone 9, but we've had two winters where the temperature got down to zone 7. So when you plant a zone 9 tree or shrub here, it'll be dead. If you want something to last a long time, you might shoot for one that can endure a zone or two lower than your listed zone.", "images": []}

If the glass is annealed then polishing after laminating is a given (or should be), but if it's heat strengthened or tempered, then....big controversy. Been to a brewery or an outdoor restaurant lately?  I love their functionality and height, but not the industrial metal appearance next to my cottage style garden.   After researching the galvanization process and the presence of zinc, I devised a plan to paint the interior and exterior of my tanks to create the aesthetic that fit my style better.  According to multiple sources, the zinc coating from the galvanization process is not harmful to people and is not dangerous to plants.  It can be detrimental if sanded and inhaled or compromised through acidic interactions.  Therefore, I chose to be extra cautious and use a food grade paint that vintners use for winemaking equipment.   After cleaning the tanks, I painted the interiors with the special ordered paint.  For the exterior, I used a metal primer paint first and then added two coats of my favorite white paint, Alabaster (Sherwin Williams).   To prepare the tanks for soil, I removed the brass drain plug on the side and drilled several 1/2 inch holes in the bottom for better drainage.  My husband laid out level flagstone bases for the tanks and set them in place.  We added a layer of pea gravel in the bottom to prevent the drainage holes from becoming clogged.  You could also use landscape fabric or pottery shards.  Next we tossed in small branches, yard clippings (chemical free), dead leaves and debris until we were about 18 inches from the top.  We finished with a mix of garden soil and compost to provide a nutrient rich growing medium.   My plants thrive in the stock tank planters, and I love how the white exterior accentuates my garden style.  I even brought one to our new house when we moved! main_question: {"author_id": "publickman", "author_name": "Lars", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/publickman", "date": "2024-03-27", "text": "I decided to start a new thread for this, in case anyone wants to make this cookie, which I really do recommend.  I think it would be just as good for Easter, even though it is traditionally made for Christmas. Melomakarona I (Greek Christmas Honey Cookies)  Yield: 24 cookies For the melomakarona For the syrup To garnish Instructions To prepare this melomakarona recipe start by making the syrup first. In a pot add all the ingredients for the syrup, besides the honey and bring to the boil. Boil for 3-4 minutes, until the sugar has dissolved and remove from the stove. Stir in the honey and set aside to cool completely. Prepare the dough for the melomakarona. In a bowl add the semolina, flour, walnuts, and baking powder and mix with a whisk to combine. In another large bowl add the orange juice, the cognac (or brandy), the sugar and spices (nutmeg, cinnamon, clove, vanilla) and mix. Add the baking soda and whisk immediately for 5-10 seconds until the ingredients combine and the baking soda dissolves and starts to foam. Pour in the bowl the water, the oil, the orange zest and honey and whisk to combine. Now it\u2019s time to combine the two mixtures. Add the mixed flour, semolina and baking powder (from step 2) in the bowl with the rest of the ingredients from step 3 and start kneading the dough for the melomakarona. Knead the dough for the melomakarona using your hands, until the ingredients combine and the dough is smooth and soft and slightly sticky. Be careful not to overwork the dough as they will become tough. Preheat the oven at 180C / 356F. Layer the bottom of 2 large baking trays with parchment paper (or Silpat) and start shaping the melomakarona. Pinch a portion of dough about the size of a walnut 30g / 1oz and shape with your palms into a smooth oblong shape, like a small egg. Place on the baking tray, push lightly the top with a fork and pierce four or five times on top about half way through the dough. Continue with the rest of the dough. Depending on how large on oven you have when your two trays are ready you can start baking them. Place the baking trays with the melomakarona in the oven and bake for approx. 20-25 minutes, until the melomakarona are lightly and evenly browned and cooked through. When the melomakarona come out of the oven, dip them immediately in the cold syrup, flipping them with a slotted spoon to absorb the syrup for approx 10-15 seconds, depending on how syrupy you like them. Remove the cookies using a slotted spoon, place in paper cupcake forms on a platter and sprinkle with chopped walnuts that have been mixed with cinnamon and clove.   If you have leftover syrup, you can drizzle that over them before adding the walnuts. Store the melomakarona at room temperature in an airtight container. They will keep for all your Christmas Holidays! Based on recipe from Eli K. WHY??? you are about 19 years late to a single trunk plant.. if you want one.. throw this one away.. and go buy such .. do not try to make this one such ... do not repot.. unless you note an actual problem that requires fixing... give it a year or two .... to get over transport shock. before you do ANYTHING ... i cant tell if its the camera.. or what not.. if its off color.. a bit yellow.. give it some highly diluted water sol fert with each watering.. jade prefer to be VERY dry.. do you have experience dealing with them.. you WILL kill it with over watering.. give us more facts so we can help ... ken", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-04-07", "text": "You can very easily prune your plant so it has a single trunk with virtually no concern that the pruning will cause the plant life threatening harm. The trick to pruning jades and portulacaria is to leave a very short stub. You don't want to cut into the node on the trunkline that gave rise to the branches you're viewing as subordinate, or competing trunks. When you leave a short stub, sealing the wound is unnecessary because the wound will dry back to the first node proximal (closer to the roots or trunk) to the cut. Once the pruning is done, in 6 months to a year you'll be able to simply rub off the desiccated tissue with your thumb, making it difficult to tell it was even pruned. Cutting flush to the lower order branch  (the branch the you're pruning is attached) or trunk will cause tissue to dry out in the immediate vicinity of the wound, such that the wound will be larger, deeper, more unsightly, and it will take longer for callus tissue to cover the wound. I would advise that you carefully cover the existing wounds with waterproof wood clue, which will prevent the wounds from growing larger due to desiccation. Use a flat toothpick or similar item to carefully paint the wound only. Try not to overlap the wound and get glue on the periderm (bark); this, because it will make a lump when the callus rolls over the glue. Al", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "gardenfanatic2003", "author_name": "gardenfanatic2003", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardenfanatic2003", "date": "2024-04-08", "text": "@ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5 generally speaking, when jade plants are getting the appropriate amount of light, their leaves will turn more of a light green or gold. Jades with dark green leaves are usually either being overfertilized or aren't receiving an appropriate amount/intensity of light, or both. However, there are different cultivars of jade which have slightly different leaves, so it's difficult to know for sure without knowing the specifics of which jade it is. Most jade plants that I see posted on plants forums or groups are very etiolated, but that one isn't, so for its first 20 years it received appropriate light. Can't say if it currently is since they grow very slowly and it likely hasn't had time to respond to its current light situation. title: Телевизионная стена в гостиной | Houzz Forum
Will a pendant light over a bathroom vanity cast shadows? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jwbadcock", "author_name": "jwbadcock", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jwbadcock", "date": "2024-03-28", "text": "We are remodeling a 1940s house built of concrete block filled with concrete. Our bathroom vanity will sit along an exterior concrete wall, so its not practical to use sconces or an over mirror light fixture. There will be recessed lighting, but good bathroom lighting is a pet peeve. Will the recessed lighting plus a pendant light cast shadows on our faces? Can anyone think of a better idea for plenty of light at the mirror that doesn't require mounting or wiring on/ in the concrete wall? I also want the bathroom to be pretty and pretty light fixtures are like jewelry!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "theresa-peterson82", "author_name": "Theresa Peterson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/theresa-peterson82", "date": "2024-03-28", "text": "Any downward light has the potential to cast shadows -- pendant light or wall-mounted sconces.  In the bathroom, your brows and nose can create shadows on the lower part of .your face. Keys to getting it right -- let's divide the lighting into tasks, and we don't really need to see a floorplan: General lighting for the bathroom -- This is for walking to the toilet, coming in to get some lotion, putting away clean towels.  The recessed lighting of which you spoke will be centered in the room, right?  This is your general lighting.  Since it'll be behind your head, it will throw big shadows on your face when you stand at the sink, but you don't really care -- you're just walking to the toilet or coming in to get your lotion or putting away clean towels.  Specific thoughts: - This should be your easiest-reach switch, as it's your most-used lighting. - I assume a 1940s house has small bathrooms, so one central light should be enough.  It is a one-room bath, right? - Since you like pretty fixtures (good for you!), this can be something nicer than a recessed pot light. - A budget-minded builder would tell you to skip this light, though it won't cost much while you already have the electrician on hand.  You could just use the vanity pendants for general lighting, but having a ceiling light is nicer. Task lighting at the sink -- I'm not sure if you're shaving or applying make-up at the sink, but the pendant lights of which you spoke will give you good, strong light in the right places.  Flank your sink with TWO pendant lights right at eye level /head level.  A single light could still throw shadows to one side, but two lights will eliminate this problem.  You can test this right now with a small lamp: hold it directly above your head, hold it just above your head and to the side, then hold it to the side of your face ... you'll see where the shadows fall.  NO to a single pendant above your head ... shadows galore.  Put them on dimmers, as their light will be \"doubled\" in the mirror.  And put them on a separate switch because you don't always want /need that strong light at the sink (like in the middle of the night). Specific lighting in the bathroom: - In addition to the above most-important lights, you also want a recessed light above /in the shower /tub area.  If you're really fighting against shadows, consider two small recessed lights on opposite ends of the shower ... as above, light from two directions will eliminate shadows.  This light will probably be combined with a fan ... don't skimp on your fan, and choose a model that'll turn itself off after X minutes. - Maybe a recessed light above the toilet.  As they aged, my grandparents (and now my parents) have all had some ... um, special medical needs at the toilet.  Extra light in this area might be useful.  Maybe not, but it won't cost you much to put it in, and then you're \"future-proof\".  At the worst, it'll make cleaning easier. - Consider a soft night light, so you can avoid turning on all these lights in the middle of the night.  You could place an outlet near the floor and run a rope light under the edge of the vanity.  Or you could place an outlet near the ceiling and hang a string of lights around the ceiling. - Yes, the type of bulb /amount of light matters, but PLACEMENT of these light fixtures matters most when we're talking about eliminating shadows.  Light of any type can only move in straight lines. - If you have a linen closet in the bathroom, add a recessed light to the front of its ceiling so you'll have good light IN that closet.", "images": []}}

E.g., and as you mentioned, a pH level not too far above 6.5 can limit the availability of Fe. An excess of any one or more of several nutrients - calcium, copper, zinc, and especially phosphorous and manganese - will also limit uptake. So, if you are or have been using a bloom-booster fertilizer you should stop. Bloom booster fertilizers all provide far more phosphorous than your plant could ever use (relative to nitrogen usage). Waterlogged grow media, soil compaction, and root congestion can also limit Fe uptake. That said, it's not a good idea to start reaching for Fe chelates to supplement the iron supply, or any other concoction aimed at supplying only one or two nutrients. Almost always it will prove to be more limiting than remedial. If you check the roots and find them badly congested, you'll need to divide the plant and repot, perhaps into a larger pot. title: Cutting Back Stems After Transplant With Plant Shock? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2024-03-30", "text": "If you transplant a shrub, expose the roots, and send the plant into shock or a death spiral, does it make sense to try to cut back the stems?   Assume the plant is one that can take a lot of trimming back safely.    The theory here is that after a \"bad\" transplant the fine roots that absorb water are damaged and cannot feed all of the leafy material on the plant.  The plant continues to lose water through its leaves through transpiration.   By cutting back the stems and removing as much leaf material as possible - exactly what percentage depends on the species - you reduce water loss by transpiration and give the plant a better chance to regrow roots before it dries out and dies.
